Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain, surpassed both his       competitors in the nobility of his extraction, which he derived       from some of the most illustrious names of the old republic. 16       But the branch from which he claimed his descent was sunk into       mean circumstances, and transplanted into a remote province. It       is difficult to form a just idea of his true character. Under the       philosophic cloak of austerity, he stands accused of concealing       most of the vices which degrade human nature. 17 But his accusers       are those venal writers who adored the fortune of Severus, and       trampled on the ashes of an unsuccessful rival. Virtue, or the       appearances of virtue, recommended Albinus to the confidence and       good opinion of Marcus; and his preserving with the son the same       interest which he had acquired with the father, is a proof at       least that he was possessed of a very flexible disposition. The       favor of a tyrant does not always suppose a want of merit in the       object of it; he may, without intending it, reward a man of worth       and ability, or he may find such a man useful to his own service.       It does not appear that Albinus served the son of Marcus, either       as the minister of his cruelties, or even as the associate of his       pleasures. He was employed in a distant honorable command, when       he received a confidential letter from the emperor, acquainting       him of the treasonable designs of some discontented generals, and       authorizing him to declare himself the guardian and successor of       the throne, by assuming the title and ensigns of Cæsar. 18 The       governor of Britain wisely declined the dangerous honor, which       would have marked him for the jealousy, or involved him in the       approaching ruin, of Commodus. He courted power by nobler, or, at       least, by more specious arts. On a premature report of the death       of the emperor, he assembled his troops; and, in an eloquent       discourse, deplored the inevitable mischiefs of despotism,       described the happiness and glory which their ancestors had       enjoyed under the consular government, and declared his firm       resolution to reinstate the senate and people in their legal       authority. This popular harangue was answered by the loud       acclamations of the British legions, and received at Rome with a       secret murmur of applause. Safe in the possession of his little       world, and in the command of an army less distinguished indeed       for discipline than for numbers and valor, 19 Albinus braved the       menaces of Commodus, maintained towards Pertinax a stately       ambiguous reserve, and instantly declared against the usurpation       of Julian. The convulsions of the capital added new weight to his       sentiments, or rather to his professions of patriotism. A regard       to decency induced him to decline the lofty titles of Augustus       and Emperor; and he imitated perhaps the example of Galba, who,       on a similar occasion, had styled himself the Lieutenant of the       senate and people. 20

Personal merit alone had raised Pescennius Niger, from an obscure       birth and station, to the government of Syria; a lucrative and       important command, which in times of civil confusion gave him a       near prospect of the throne. Yet his parts seem to have been       better suited to the second than to the first rank; he was an       unequal rival, though he might have approved himself an excellent       lieutenant, to Severus, who afterwards displayed the greatness of       his mind by adopting several useful institutions from a       vanquished enemy. 21 In his government Niger acquired the esteem       of the soldiers and the love of the provincials. His rigid       discipline fortified the valor and confirmed the obedience of the       former, whilst the voluptuous Syrians were less delighted with       the mild firmness of his administration, than with the affability       of his manners, and the apparent pleasure with which he attended       their frequent and pompous festivals. 22 As soon as the       intelligence of the atrocious murder of Pertinax had reached       Antioch, the wishes of Asia invited Niger to assume the Imperial       purple and revenge his death. The legions of the eastern frontier       embraced his cause; the opulent but unarmed provinces, from the       frontiers of Æthiopia 23 to the Hadriatic, cheerfully submitted       to his power; and the kings beyond the Tigris and the Euphrates       congratulated his election, and offered him their homage and       services. The mind of Niger was not capable of receiving this       sudden tide of fortune: he flattered himself that his accession       would be undisturbed by competition and unstained by civil blood;       and whilst he enjoyed the vain pomp of triumph, he neglected to       secure the means of victory. Instead of entering into an       effectual negotiation with the powerful armies of the West, whose       resolution might decide, or at least must balance, the mighty       contest; instead of advancing without delay towards Rome and       Italy, where his presence was impatiently expected, 24 Niger       trifled away in the luxury of Antioch those irretrievable moments       which were diligently improved by the decisive activity of       Severus. 25

The country of Pannonia and Dalmatia, which occupied the space       between the Danube and the Hadriatic, was one of the last and       most difficult conquests of the Romans. In the defence of       national freedom, two hundred thousand of these barbarians had       once appeared in the field, alarmed the declining age of       Augustus, and exercised the vigilant prudence of Tiberius at the       head of the collected force of the empire. 26 The Pannonians       yielded at length to the arms and institutions of Rome. Their       recent subjection, however, the neighborhood, and even the       mixture, of the unconquered tribes, and perhaps the climate,       adapted, as it has been observed, to the production of great       bodies and slow minds, 27 all contributed to preserve some       remains of their original ferocity, and under the tame and       uniform countenance of Roman provincials, the hardy features of       the natives were still to be discerned. Their warlike youth       afforded an inexhaustible supply of recruits to the legions       stationed on the banks of the Danube, and which, from a perpetual       warfare against the Germans and Sarmazans, were deservedly       esteemed the best troops in the service.

The Pannonian army was at this time commanded by Septimius       Severus, a native of Africa, who, in the gradual ascent of       private honors, had concealed his daring ambition, which was       never diverted from its steady course by the allurements of       pleasure, the apprehension of danger, or the feelings of       humanity. 28 On the first news of the murder of Pertinax, he       assembled his troops, painted in the most lively colors the       crime, the insolence, and the weakness of the Prætorian guards,       and animated the legions to arms and to revenge. He concluded       (and the peroration was thought extremely eloquent) with       promising every soldier about four hundred pounds; an honorable       donative, double in value to the infamous bribe with which Julian       had purchased the empire. 29 The acclamations of the army       immediately saluted Severus with the names of Augustus, Pertinax,       and Emperor; and he thus attained the lofty station to which he       was invited, by conscious merit and a long train of dreams and       omens, the fruitful offsprings either of his superstition or       policy. 30

30 (return) [ Herodian, l. ii. p. 78. Severus was declared       emperor on the banks of the Danube, either at Carnuntum,       according to Spartianus, (Hist. August. p. 65,) or else at       Sabaria, according to Victor. Mr. Hume, in supposing that the       birth and dignity of Severus were too much inferior to the       Imperial crown, and that he marched into Italy as general only,       has not considered this transaction with his usual accuracy,       (Essay on the original contract.) * Note: Carnuntum, opposite to       the mouth of the Morava: its position is doubtful, either       Petronel or Haimburg. A little intermediate village seems to       indicate by its name (Altenburg) the site of an old town.       D’Anville Geogr. Anc. Sabaria, now Sarvar.—G. Compare note       37.—M.]

### Main Argument

The passage surveys the chaotic succession struggles of the early 3rd century and evaluates three would‑be emperors—Clodius Albinus, Pescennius Niger and Septimius Severus—through the lens of personal character, political opportunism, and the decisive influence of the army.  

1. **Albinus** is presented as a noble, well‑born Briton whose “flexible disposition” and refusal of tyrannical titles reveal a cautious, perhaps overly moderate, nature. He declines the dangerous claim to the throne, yet his “popular harangue” before the British legions shows he can rally support when he chooses.  
2. **Niger** is depicted as a capable administrator in the east who enjoys the love of provincials and the respect of soldiers, but his indecision and luxury in Antioch cost him the chance to secure the western armies. He is thus an “unequal rival” whose ambition is outmatched by circumstance.  
3. **Severus** emerges as the decisive, ruthless commander who seizes the moment after Pertinax’s murder, promises generous donatives, and wins the loyalty of the Danubian legions. The narrator’s tone shifts from restrained praise to admiration for his “conscious merit” and “long train of dreams and omens,” suggesting that in a time of crisis, military backing and bold action outweigh noble restraint.

Implicitly, the narrator argues that **the legitimacy of imperial rule in this period is inseparable from military support and personal ambition**. Noble birth alone does not guarantee success; moral virtue may be present, but decisive, often ruthless, action determines who ultimately holds power.

### Rhetorical Style

Herodian’s narration employs several classic rhetorical devices:

- **Moral Evaluation and Contrast** – The text constantly pits “virtue” against “vice” (e.g., Albinus’s “flexible disposition” versus the “venial writers” who slander him). This moralizing frames the political actors within a ethical spectrum.
- **Use of Direct Speech and Vivid Imagery** – Phrases such as “deplored the inevitable mischiefs of despotism” and “declared his firm resolution” give the passage a dramatic, almost oratorical quality.
- **Parallelism and Antithesis** – Comparisons like “the favor of a tyrant does not always suppose a want of merit” and the juxtaposition of “Albinus’s reserve” versus “Severus’s boldness” create rhythmic balance and emphasize contrasts.
- **Allusion to Authority** – Frequent citations of earlier sources (e.g., “Herodian, l. ii. p. 78”) and references to Roman tradition (the “consular government,” “senate and people”) lend the narrative an air of scholarly credibility.
- **Hyperbolic Praise/Bland Irony** – The description of Severus’s donative as “double in value to the infamous bribe” heightens the sense of his magnanimity, while the narrator’s occasional irony (e.g., calling accusers “venal writers”) subtly undermines flattery.

Overall, the style is **formal, measured and morally didactic**, suited to the conventions of ancient historiography: it reports events, judges motives, and offers a lesson on the perils of civil war.

### Historical Context

The passage reflects the turmoil of the **Year of the Five Emperors (AD 193)** and its immediate aftermath:

- **Political Fragmentation** – After Commodus’s assassination, the empire lacks a clear, accepted successor. Albinus, governing Britain, and Niger, commanding the eastern provinces, each consider themselves legitimate heirs.
- **Rise of the Army as Power Broker** – Military loyalty is the decisive factor. Albinus’s “premature report of the death of the emperor” prompts him to gather troops; Severus’s “promising every soldier about four hundred pounds” secures the Danubian legions’ acclamation.
- **Geographic Scope** – The narrative moves from Britain to the eastern frontiers (Syria, Antioch) and the Danube, illustrating the empire’s vast, yet thinly administered, borders during this crisis.
- **Cultural Values** – The historian repeatedly invokes “the happiness and glory which their ancestors enjoyed under the consular government,” expressing a nostalgia for Republican virtues amid increasing despotism.
- **Severan Re‑orientation** – By portraying Severus as the successful, ambitious commander, Herodian subtly foreshadows the Severan dynasty’s shift toward a more militarized, autocratic rule, a trend that would dominate Roman history for the next half‑century.

Thus, the text is not merely a chronicle of events; it is a **contemporary Roman assessment of how personal ambition, military might, and moral character intersected in a fractured empire**, using rhetorical tools honed in the historiographical tradition.

Herodian, a Roman historian, crafts a nuanced yet morally charged account of three imperial claimants. 3. **The fatal consequence of imperial weakness.**

Even this spectacular display of authority only temporarily restores order; the deeper problem—soldiers who no longer respect the law—remains.  Gibbon reads this whole episode as evidence of the “deplorable weakness of government” that makes the empire vulnerable to internal collapse.

In short, Gibbon argues that by the time of Alexander Severus the Roman state has become a “government of the soldiers,” and the emperor’s only recourse is to hide his weakness behind patience and dissimulation. 2. **Correcting a factual slip about Dion.**  
   Dion Cassius, far from being a wealthy man with estates in Campania, was a relatively poor historian who only mentions that the emperor permitted him to spend part of his consular term outside Rome and later to retire to his native city of Nice in Bithynia.  Gibbon’s implication that Dion “spent the greatest part of his consulship at his villas in Campania” is therefore an anachronistic embellishment.

It seldom exceeded one       _per cent_.; but it comprehended whatever was sold in the markets       or by public auction, from the most considerable purchases of       lands and houses, to those minute objects which can only derive a       value from their infinite multitude and daily consumption. Such a       tax, as it affects the body of the people, has ever been the       occasion of clamor and discontent. An emperor well acquainted       with the wants and resources of the state was obliged to declare,       by a public edict, that the support of the army depended in a       great measure on the produce of the excise. 101

III. When Augustus resolved to establish a permanent military       force for the defence of his government against foreign and       domestic enemies, he instituted a peculiar treasury for the pay       of the soldiers, the rewards of the veterans, and the       extra-ordinary expenses of war. The ample revenue of the excise,       though peculiarly appropriated to those uses, was found       inadequate. To supply the deficiency, the emperor suggested a new       tax of five per cent. on all legacies and inheritances. But the       nobles of Rome were more tenacious of property than of freedom.       Their indignant murmurs were received by Augustus with his usual       temper. He candidly referred the whole business to the senate,       and exhorted them to provide for the public service by some other       expedient of a less odious nature. They were divided and       perplexed. He insinuated to them, that their obstinacy would       oblige him to _propose_ a general land tax and capitation. They       acquiesced in silence. 102 The new imposition on legacies and       inheritances was, however, mitigated by some restrictions. It did       not take place unless the object was of a certain value, most       probably of fifty or a hundred pieces of gold; 103 nor could it       be exacted from the nearest of kin on the father’s side. 104 When       the rights of nature and poverty were thus secured, it seemed       reasonable, that a stranger, or a distant relation, who acquired       an unexpected accession of fortune, should cheerfully resign a       twentieth part of it, for the benefit of the state. 105

Such a tax, plentiful as it must prove in every wealthy       community, was most happily suited to the situation of the       Romans, who could frame their arbitrary wills, according to the       dictates of reason or caprice, without any restraint from the       modern fetters of entails and settlements. A servile       crowd, in which he frequently reckoned prætors and consuls,       courted his smiles, pampered his avarice, applauded his follies,       served his passions, and waited with impatience for his death.       The arts of attendance and flattery were formed into a most       lucrative science; those who professed it acquired a peculiar       appellation; and the whole city, according to the lively       descriptions of satire, was divided between two parties, the       hunters and their game. 107 Yet, while so many unjust and       extravagant wills were every day dictated by cunning and       subscribed by folly, a few were the result of rational esteem and       virtuous gratitude. Cicero, who had so often defended the lives       and fortunes of his fellow-citizens, was rewarded with legacies       to the amount of a hundred and seventy thousand pounds; 108 nor       do the friends of the younger Pliny seem to have been less       generous to that amiable orator. 109 Whatever was the motive of       the testator, the treasury claimed, without distinction, the       twentieth part of his estate: and in the course of two or three       generations, the whole property of the subject must have       gradually passed through the coffers of the state.

In the first and golden years of the reign of Nero, that prince,       from a desire of popularity, and perhaps from a blind impulse of       benevolence, conceived a wish of abolishing the oppression of the       customs and excise. The mildness and precision of their laws ascertained the rule and       measure of taxation, and protected the subject of every rank       against arbitrary interpretations, antiquated claims, and the       insolent vexation of the farmers of the revenue. 111 For it is       somewhat singular, that, in every age, the best and wisest of the       Roman governors persevered in this pernicious method of       collecting the principal branches at least of the excise and       customs. 112

The sentiments, and, indeed, the situation, of Caracalla were       very different from those of the Antonines. Inattentive, or       rather averse, to the welfare of his people, he found himself       under the necessity of gratifying the insatiate avarice which he       had excited in the army. As its influence was       not confined to Rome or Italy, the produce continually increased       with the gradual extension of the Roman City. The new citizens,       though charged, on equal terms, 113 with the payment of new       taxes, which had not affected them as subjects, derived an ample       compensation from the rank they obtained, the privileges they       acquired, and the fair prospect of honors and fortune that was       thrown open to their ambition. When all the provincials became liable to the peculiar       impositions of Roman citizens, they seemed to acquire a legal       exemption from the tributes which they had paid in their former       condition of subjects. Such were not the maxims of government       adopted by Caracalla and his pretended son. The old as well as       the new taxes were, at the same time, levied in the provinces. It       was reserved for the virtue of Alexander to relieve them in a       great measure from this intolerable grievance, by reducing the       tributes to a thirteenth part of the sum exacted at the time of       his accession. 115 It is impossible to conjecture the motive that       engaged him to spare so trifling a remnant of the public evil;       but the noxious weed, which had not been totally eradicated,       again sprang up with the most luxuriant growth, and in the       succeeding age darkened the Roman world with its deadly shade. In       the course of this history, we shall be too often summoned to       explain the land tax, the capitation, and the heavy contributions       of corn, wine, oil, and meat, which were exacted from the       provinces for the use of the court, the army, and the capital.

As long as Rome and Italy were respected as the centre of       government, a national spirit was preserved by the ancient, and       insensibly imbibed by the adopted, citizens. The principal       commands of the army were filled by men who had received a       liberal education, were well instructed in the advantages of laws       and letters, and who had risen, by equal steps, through the       regular succession of civil and military honors. 116 To their       influence and example we may partly ascribe the modest obedience       of the legions during the two first centuries of the Imperial       history.

But when the last enclosure of the Roman constitution was       trampled down by Caracalla, the separation of professions       gradually succeeded to the distinction of ranks. The more       polished citizens of the internal provinces were alone qualified       to act as lawyers and magistrates. The rougher trade of arms was       abandoned to the peasants and barbarians of the frontiers, who       knew no country but their camp, no science but that of war, no       civil laws, and scarcely those of military discipline. With       bloody hands, savage manners, and desperate resolutions, they       sometimes guarded, but much oftener subverted, the throne of the       emperors.

Of the various forms of government which have prevailed in the       world, an hereditary monarchy seems to present the fairest scope       for ridicule. Is it possible to relate without an indignant       smile, that, on the father’s decease, the property of a nation,       like that of a drove of oxen, descends to his infant son, as yet       unknown to mankind and to himself; and that the bravest warriors       and the wisest statesmen, relinquishing their natural right to       empire, approach the royal cradle with bended knees and       protestations of inviolable fidelity? Satire and declamation may       paint these obvious topics in the most dazzling colors, but our       more serious thoughts will respect a useful prejudice, that       establishes a rule of succession, independent of the passions of       mankind; and we shall cheerfully acquiesce in any expedient which       deprives the multitude of the dangerous, and indeed the ideal,       power of giving themselves a master.

Maximin, for that was his name, though born on the territories of       the empire, descended from a mixed race of barbarians. His father       was a Goth, and his mother of the nation of the Alani. ### I. Overview  

The passage is a compact, highly rhetorical narrative that moves from a vivid anecdote about a Thracian wrestler (the “future Maximin”) to a sustained moral‑political critique of the early‑third‑century imperial crisis. He then sketches Maximin’s biographical background, his relationship with the army, and the circumstances of his revolt against Emperor Alexander Severus. The passage culminates in a stark condemnation of Maximin’s cruelty, framed as the inevitable outcome of a militarised empire in which the soldiers’ discontent fuels the ambition of a barbarian usurper.

### II. Main Argument  

1. **The Army as the Engine of Imperial Change**  
   - Tacitus argues that the *discontent* of the troops, not the emperor’s personal failings alone, is the decisive factor in Maximin’s ascent. The soldiers, weary of “the vexatious discipline imposed by an effeminate Syrian” (Alexander), turn to Maximin as a “real soldier… educated in camps, exercised in war” (line ~).

2. **Barbarian Origin as Moral Defect**  
   - Maximin’s “mixed race” (Gothic father, Alani mother) and “savage appearance” are repeatedly highlighted (lines ~). Tacitus presents these as *moral* shortcomings—lack of Romanitas, ignorance of civil institutions, and a propensity for cruelty.  
   - The passage echoes Tacitus’s elsewhere‑stated judgment that *“the empire is no longer ruled by men of Roman blood, but by those born of the provinces”* (cf. *Annals* II.61).  

3. **The Usurper’s Cruelty Derived from Fear of Contempt**  
   - Maximin’s “fear of contempt” (line ~) drives his ruthless treatment of perceived ingrates (the “benefactors” who once helped him). Tacitus frames his violence not merely as personal cruelty but as a political calculus: “he published, in characters of blood, the indelible history of his baseness and ingratitude.”  
   - This underlines Tacitus’s moral thesis that *“the more a ruler despises his subjects, the more he provokes them to rebellion”*—a principle that recurs throughout his work.  

4. **The Vexed Relationship Between Emperor and Senate**  
   - Alexander is portrayed as a “timid slave of his mother and of the senate,” a ruler emasculated by “effeminate insults.” Tacitus implies that Alexander’s weakness alienates the army, making him vulnerable to usurpers.  
   - This reflects Tacitus’s broader critique of *soft* imperial rule (cf. his condemnation of Nero’s “effeminacy” in *Annals* XII.31).  

5. **A Cautionary Exempla for Future Readers**  
   - The wrestling episode serves as a *warning*: a “young barbarian… earnestly solicited… that he might be allowed to contend for the prize of wrestling” (line ~). His subsequent rise foreshadows the danger of allowing “foreigners” into positions of military authority.  

In sum, Tacitus’s argument is that Maximin’s usurpation is the logical, albeit tragic, consequence of a militarised empire in which the army’s discontent, the emperor’s weakness, and the usurper’s barbarian origins converge to produce a regime of cruelty and instability.

### IV. Historical Context  

1. **The Early‑Third‑Century Crisis**  
   - The passage reflects the *Year of the Six Emperors* (AD 238‑244). Maximin (originally “Maximinus Thracus”) seized power after the death of Alexander Severus, inaugurating a period of rapid succession and civil war.

   - Maximin’s mixed Gothic‑Alani background illustrates the growing *Romanisation* of provincial elites. Tacitus’s moral condemnation reflects a Roman bias that values *Romanitas* over ethnic origin—a bias evident in earlier works such as Livy’s *Ab Urbe Condita* (e.g., the “Latins as Romans”).

   - Tacitus’s use of the wrestling anecdote as a *foreshadowing* device resonates with his method of embedding moral lessons within specific historical episodes (cf. *Annals* II.12 on the death of Germanicus).

   - “The troops listened with pleasure to the emissaries of Maximin. **They blushed at their own ignominious patience**, which, during thirteen years, had supported the vexatious discipline imposed by an effeminate Syrian, the timid slave of his mother and of the senate.”

When he reluctantly accepted the       purple, he was above fourscore years old; a last and valuable       remains of the happy age of the Antonines, whose virtues he       revived in his own conduct, and celebrated in an elegant poem of       thirty books. His manners were less pure, but his character       was equally amiable with that of his father. As soon as the Gordians had appeased the first tumult of a       popular election, they removed their court to Carthage. These       considerations, and perhaps others of a more private nature, were       debated in a previous conference of the consuls and the       magistrates. Carthage, destitute of defence,       opened her gates to the conqueror, and Africa was exposed to the       rapacious cruelty of a slave, obliged to satisfy his unrelenting       master with a large account of blood and treasure. 26

The fate of the Gordians filled Rome with just but unexpected       terror. A silent consternation prevailed in the       assembly, till a senator, of the name and family of Trajan,       awakened his brethren from their fatal lethargy. ### 1. Main Argument

The passage is a learned exposition of the Zoroastrian doctrine of *dualism*—the belief that the universe is the product of two eternal, opposing principles, **Ormuzd** (the benevolent principle of Light and Good) and **Ahriman** (the malevolent principle of Darkness and Evil). The author’s chief claim can be summed up in three inter‑locking points:

1. **Philosophical Innovation** – Zoroastrianism’s “celebrated doctrine of the two principles” is presented as a bold, “injudicious” attempt by Eastern thought to reconcile the existence of moral and physical evil with a beneficent Creator. In other words, the text argues that the dualistic schema is an original philosophical solution, not a mere copy of Greek or Chaldaic ideas.

2. **Cosmic History and the Conflict of Good and Evil** – Ormuzd creates a perfect, luminous world (the “egg”) and bestows upon humanity the capacity for virtue. Ahriman, however, “pierces Ormuzd’s egg,” injecting darkness into the otherwise harmonious cosmos. From that rupture, “the most minute articles of good and evil are intimately intermingled,” producing a perpetual state of tension: poisonous plants among salutary ones, earthquakes and floods, the “conflict of Nature,” and the continual suffering of humanity.

3. **Eschatological Resolution** – The text asserts that the “enlightened wisdom of goodness” will ultimately render Ormuzd’s power superior to Ahriman’s malice. In the final age, Ahriman and his followers will be subdued, returning to darkness, while virtue will restore “the eternal peace and harmony of the universe.” The passage also anticipates a nuanced doctrinal stance: contrary to some interpretations, Ahriman was originally “born good” and only became evil through envy (see footnote 1002). In the Zend‑Avesta he will be defeated, purified, and finally united with Ormuzd in a harmonious kingdom.

Thus, the central argument is that Zoroastrian dualism provides a coherent philosophical framework for explaining the coexistence of evil, that the ongoing cosmic war between Light and Darkness is both historically grounded in myth and theologically necessary, and that an eventual triumph of Ormuzd over Ahriman promises universal restoration.

| **Hyperbole** | “the sin not inferior in guilt to the violation of the moral duties”; “your good works … exceed in number the leaves of the trees, the drops of rain, the stars in the heaven, or the sands on the sea‑shore.” | Exaggerates to stress the seriousness of ritual neglect or the magnitude of good works. |
| **Rhetorical question / Conditional hypothesis** | “Had Zoroaster, in all his institutions, invariably supported this exalted character?” | Invites the reader to imagine an alternate, ideal version of Zoroaster, thereby emphasizing what is missing in the actual tradition. |
| **Appeal to authority (ethos)** | Frequent citations of Gibbon, Hyde, Foucher, and the “Sadder” as sources. | Lends scholarly weight to the author’s claims about Zoroastrian origins and later priestly accretions. |
| **Alliteration** | “fasting and celibacy,” “humblest but most useful.” | Adds a musical quality that draws attention to key phrases. |
| **Repetition** | “The moral duties … were required,” “the saint … is obliged,” “the Magi … were extremely numerous,” etc. | Reinforces central ideas and creates a rhythmic, persuasive flow. |
| **Personification** | “the saint … is obliged to beget children, to plant useful trees.” | Gives the abstract moral requirement a human, active voice, making it feel more immediate. |
| **Exemplum (illustrative anecdote)** | The description of the annual festival where the king dines with husbandmen, hears petitions, and speaks of mutual dependence. | Provides a concrete, vivid case study that exemplifies the moral‑social ideals the author praises. |
| **Inclusive language / “we‑statement”** | “From your labors we receive our subsistence; you derive your tranquillity from our vigilance … let us live together like brothers in concord and love.” | Creates a sense of communal solidarity and shared responsibility. |
| **Amplification (expansion of a point)** | Detailed enumeration of the Magi’s property, taxes, hierarchy, and the priest‑teacher’s claim to know “all things” and “deliver all men.” | Overloads the notion of priestly power, underscoring how later superstition swelled from the original teachings. |

*Taken together, these devices work to present Zoroastrianism as a morally‑oriented, human‑centered religion whose later priesthoods layered unnecessary ritual and superstition on top of its original, practical teachings.*

But the active victor, at the head of       a numerous and disciplined army, visited in person every province       of Persia. The defeat of the boldest rebels, and the reduction of       the strongest fortifications, 33 diffused the terror of his arms,       and prepared the way for the peaceful reception of his authority.       An obstinate resistance was fatal to the chiefs; but their       followers were treated with lenity. 34 A cheerful submission was       rewarded with honors and riches, but the prudent Artaxerxes,       suffering no person except himself to assume the title of king,       abolished every intermediate power between the throne and the       people. A forty years’ tranquillity, the fruit of valor and       moderation, had succeeded the victories of Trajan. During the       period that elapsed from the accession of Marcus to the reign of       Alexander, the Roman and the Parthian empires were twice engaged       in war; and although the whole strength of the Arsacides       contended with a part only of the forces of Rome, the event was       most commonly in favor of the latter. The second paragraph belongs to a broader, trans‑national scientific controversy:

The passage is a **micro‑cosm of early‑19th‑century German scholarship**: it attempts to answer two interlocking questions—*who were the ancient peoples of Germany?* and *what does the ancient description of the Baltic tell us about modern geology?*—by **collecting classical testimonia, citing contemporary philologists, and juxtaposing Swedish “catastrophist” ideas with Lyell’s uniformitarianism**.  

Stylistically, the author employs a **balanced, source‑critical rhetoric**: enumeration, appeal to authority, conditional language, and a measured presentation of disagreement. Historically, the text reflects:

* the **national‑cultural imagination** that turned ancient ethnography into a foundation myth, and

In sum, the passage illustrates how **classical antiquity was being re‑interpreted not merely as a source of antiquarian lore but as a framework for contemporary nation‑building and for emerging earth‑science**. The author’s cautious, citation‑rich style is precisely what made such interdisciplinary synthesis possible in the German academy of the early 19th century.

He fixed generals of ability in       the several stations of attack, and assumed in person the conduct       of the most important province on the Upper Danube. After a long       and doubtful conflict, the spirit of the barbarians was subdued.       The Quadi and the Marcomanni, 83 who had taken the lead in the       war, were the most severely punished in its catastrophe. They       were commanded to retire five miles 84 from their own banks of       the Danube, and to deliver up the flower of the youth, who were       immediately sent into Britain, a remote island, where they might       be secure as hostages, and useful as soldiers. 85 On the frequent       rebellions of the Quadi and Marcomanni, the irritated emperor       resolved to reduce their country into the form of a province. This formidable league,       however, the only one that appears in the two first centuries of       the Imperial history, was entirely dissipated, without leaving       any traces behind in Germany.

The dissolution of an ancient       confederacy restored to the independent tribes their peculiar but       long-forgotten appellation. A victorious state often communicated       its own name to a vanquished people. Wars, and the administration of public affairs, are the principal       subjects of history; but the number of persons interested in       these busy scenes is very different, according to the different       condition of mankind. **Rhetorical Analysis of Text 90**  

---

### 1. Overview  

Text 90 is a compact but highly learned passage that blends geography, ethnography, military history and moral commentary to trace the migration of the Goths (and allied peoples) from their Germanic heartland to the Danube frontier and finally into the Roman province of Moesia. The author moves from a mythic “great enterprise” to a detailed description of the Ukrainian steppe, then to a political‑military narrative of the Gothic incursions under Decius. Throughout the passage the writer constantly invokes classical authorities (Strabo, Tacitus, Pliny, etc.), enumerates tribal names, and juxtaposes natural abundance with human “idleness and rapine.” The passage is therefore a classic example of late‑antique/early‑medieval historiography: a scholarly narrative that uses rhetorical devices to establish authority (ethos), to persuade the reader of a moral lesson (pathos), and to present a logical, evidence‑based argument (logos).

---

### 2. Rhetorical Devices  

| Device | Example | Function |
|--------|---------|----------|
| **Anaphora / Enumeration** | “the Peucini, the Borani, the Carpi, &c.” (25) | Creates a sense of exhaustive classification; signals that the Goths’ origins are complex and disputed. |
| **Parallelism** | “fixed huts or movable tents, … close dress or flowing garments, … marriage of one or of several wives, … infantry or cavalry, … Teutonic or Sclavonian language” (27) | Groups similar oppositions, making the contrast between Germanic and Sarmatian cultures clear and memorable. |
| **Antithesis** | “the plenty of game … all displayed the liberality of Nature, and tempted the industry of man” vs. “the Goths withstood all these temptations, and still adhered to a life of idleness, of poverty, and of rapine.” | Highlights the paradox of abundance and moral failure; underscores the moral didactic tone. |
| **Hyperbole** | “the bravest warriors from all the Vandalic states of Germany,” “the great enterprise” (1) | Elevates the Goths to epic status, creating an aura of heroic destiny. |
| **Rhetorical Question** | “If we inquire into the characteristic marks of the people of Germany and of Sarmatia…” (27) | Directs the reader’s attention to the logical basis of the author’s ethnic classification; invites assent. |
| **Metaphor/Imagery** | “liberality of Nature,” “tempted the industry of man,” “the vast tract of land … wasted by the Venedi” (24) | Personifies the environment and the peoples, making the geography feel alive and the ethnic distinctions vivid. |
| **Allusion to Classical Authority** | Footnote chain (Strabo, Tacitus, Pliny, Ptolemy, Dion, Livy, Plutarch, Diodorus Siculus, Adelung) (251) | Establishes scholarly credibility (ethos) and signals that the narrative is part of a longer, authoritative tradition. |
| **Chiasmus / Inverted Parallelism** | “by a close dress or flowing garments, by the marriage of one or of several wives” (27) | Emphasizes the contrast between “Germanic” orderliness and “Sarmatian” variability. |
| **Lexical Contrast (positive vs. negative)** | “abundant game, fish, bee‑hives… the liberality of Nature” vs. “idleness, poverty, rapine” (28) | Evokes a moral polarity that serves both descriptive and didactic purposes. |
| **Use of Superscript Numbers (citation markers)** | “22”, “23”, “24”, “25”, “251”, “28”, “29” | Provides a scholarly scaffolding; signals that the text is a compilation of earlier sources, not a contemporary eyewitness account. |

---

### 3. Descriptive Language  

1. **Geographic Imagery** – The steppe is rendered almost poetically:  
   *“the windings of that great stream through the plains of Poland and Russia gave a direction to their line of march, and a constant supply of fresh water and pasturage to their numerous herds of cattle.”*  
   The “windings,” “fresh water,” and “numerous herds” create a vivid tableau of a pastoral, river‑driven landscape that both sustains and tempts the migrating warriors.

2. **Natural Bounty vs. Human Failure** – The author repeatedly juxtaposes “plenty,” “liberality of Nature,” “industry,” with the Goths’ “idleness,” “poverty,” and “rapine.” This contrast is not merely descriptive; it is moral, implying that the Goths squander the gifts of the earth.

3. **Ethnic Markers as Physical/Cultural Signifiers** – The passage lists “fixed huts or movable tents,” “close dress or flowing garments,” and “marriage of one or several wives.” These are not neutral observations but rhetorical markers that the author uses to draw a line between “Germanic” orderliness and “Sarmatian” fluidity.

4. **Militaristic Imagery** – “Infantry or cavalry,” “the numerous herds of cattle,” “the numerous detachments scattered devastation,” and “the main body of the army, consisting of seventy thousand Germans and Sarmatians” all serve to underline the scale and composition of the Gothic force.

5. **Temporal and Moral Framing** – Phrases such as “the fame of a great enterprise excited the bravest warriors,” “confident in their valor, and careless of whatever power might oppose their progress,” and “the Goths withstood all these temptations” set a tone of heroic confidence that is undercut by the moral condemnation of their subsequent idleness.

---

### 4. Historical Context  

| Aspect | Textual Reference | Real‑World Correspondence |
|--------|-------------------|---------------------------|
| **Gothic Migration** | “The first motions of the emigrants carried them to the banks of the Prypec… they followed the unknown course of the river…” | Early 1st‑century AD movements of the Greco‑Celtic “Goths” (often called *Scythian* or *Sarmatian* in Roman sources) toward the Danube basin. |
| **Ethnic Ambiguity** | Discusses whether the Bastarnæ are Germanic, Sarmatian, or Gallic; cites Strabo, Tacitus, Pliny, etc. | Historians debated the origins of the *Bastarnae* and related peoples; the passage reflects that scholarly uncertainty. |
| **Trajan’s Dacia** | “The conquests of Trajan… weakened the empire on that side… the new and unsettled province of Dacia was neither strong enough to resist, nor rich enough to satiate the rapaciousness of the barbarians.” | Trajan’s Dacian Wars (101‑106 AD) and the subsequent Roman administration of Moesia. |
| **Irruption under Decius (c. 250 AD)** | “Cnīva, king of the Goths… passed the Danube a second time… the inhabitants consented to ransom… the invaders retreated back into their deserts…” | The Gothic incursion that forced Emperor Decius (250 AD) to negotiate with the barbarians; the battle at Marcianopolis (239 AD) and the later “Battle of the Catalaunian Plains” are later stages of this process. |
| **Use of Classical Sources** | Frequent footnote citations; footnote “G.” (likely a marginal note by a 6th‑century scribe). | The passage is a product of the *Barbarian* historiographical tradition that relied heavily on Greek and Latin writers (Strabo, Tacitus, Pliny, etc.) to legitimize its ethnographic claims. |

The text therefore belongs to the **late‑antique/early‑medieval historiographical tradition** that sought to explain the “origins” of the peoples who threatened the Roman frontiers. The author is not merely recounting events; he is constructing an **ethnological framework** that attempts to locate the Goths within a broader Germanic‑Sarmatian spectrum, thereby providing a moral and political explanation for their incursions.

---

### 5. Nature of the Source  

1. **Primary vs. Secondary** – The passage is **secondary** in the strict sense. It is a *synthetic* work that quotes and evaluates earlier authors (Strabo, Tacitus, Pliny, etc.). The superscript numbers and marginal notes (e.g., “G.”) are typical of medieval manuscript scholarship, indicating that the text has been **annotated and revised** over centuries.

2. **Genre and Purpose** – The style resembles that of a **learned chronicle or ethnohistorical treatise** (cf. Jordanes’ *Getica*, Procopius’ *History of the Wars*). Its purpose is threefold:  
   - **Ethno‑historical explanation** (why the Goths moved, what their origins were).  
   - **Moral didacticism** (the Goths’ hubris, idleness, and rapacity as a warning).  
   - **Political commentary** (the vulnerability of the Danubian frontier under Roman rule).

3. **Bias and Agenda** –  
   - **Ethnic bias:** The author tries to locate the Goths in a *Germanic* tradition but simultaneously acknowledges a *Sarmatian* component, suggesting a desire to **reconcile** rather than **polarise** ethnic identities.  
   - **Moral bias:** The Goths are portrayed as **confident yet morally bankrupt**—a classic “barbarian” stereotype that serves both narrative drama and moral instruction.  
   - **Roman‑centric perspective:** The Roman administration is depicted as **weak** (poorly guarded Danube forts, reliance on local levies) while the Goths are cast as **unstoppable** forces of conquest. This reflects a **post‑imperial viewpoint** that seeks to explain Roman decline through the “barbarian” threat.

4. **Reliability** – The reliance on classical authors (who themselves were often polemical) and the lack of contemporary eyewitness testimony diminish the passage’s factual reliability. However, its **critical apparatus** (footnotes, marginal commentary) shows a **self‑awareness** about the uncertain ethnic geography, which lends it a scholarly veneer.

---

### 6. Overall Rhetorical Effect  

The passage succeeds in **weaving three rhetorical strands** into a cohesive narrative:

1. **Ethos** – By sprinkling the text with citations of Strabo, Tacitus, Pliny, and later scholars, the author positions himself as a learned interpreter of “ancient” authority. The footnote apparatus also signals a scholarly community that validates his conclusions.

2. **Pathos** – Vivid natural imagery (the “liberality of Nature”) juxtaposed with the moral condemnation of the Goths’ idleness creates an emotional tension that engages the reader’s sense of wonder and moral judgment.

3. **Logos** – The systematic classification of peoples, the enumeration of migrations, and the logical deduction (“If we inquire… we shall discover…”) provide a rational framework that makes the ethnic and political claims appear inevitable rather than arbitrary.

Through **parallelism, antithesis, hyperbole, and metaphor**, the author not only tells a story of movement and conquest but also **frames it as a moral lesson**: the abundance of the steppe was squandered by a people that lacked restraint, leading them to “rapine” and ultimately to the disastrous incursion into Roman territory. The passage thus functions as a **didactic historiography**, using rhetorical artifice to both explain and judge the actions of the Goths.

---

### 7. Conclusion  

Text 90 exemplifies the rhetorical strategies typical of early medieval historiography: a learned narrative that blends geography, ethnography, and moral commentary while constantly invoking classical authority. Its descriptive language is lush yet purposeful—natural bounty is rendered almost poetic, only to be contrasted with the Goths’ moral failure. The historical context of 1st‑3rd‑century Dacia and the Gothic incursions under Decius provides the factual backbone, while the author’s bias toward a Germanic‑Sarmatian synthesis and his moral condemnation of barbarism shape the argument. Because the passage is heavily mediated through earlier sources and is marked by extensive footnoting, it should be read as a **secondary, scholarly reconstruction** rather than a contemporary eyewitness account. Nonetheless, its rhetorical skill—clear enumeration, balanced antithesis, vivid metaphor, and the strategic deployment of ethos—makes it an effective vehicle for both explaining the Gothic migrations and delivering a moral warning about the perils of hubristic, rapacious peoples.

**Answer 98 – Historical “facts” the passage tries to convey**

**Text 99 – “The voice of history… Sapor and Gallienus”**  

---

## 1. Main Argument (Thesis)

The passage argues that the traditional accounts of the Persian king Sapor’s treatment of the captured Roman Emperor Valerian, and of the later reign of Gallienus, are exaggerated or unreliable.  The author wants us to see that:

1. **Historical memory is often a tool of propaganda** – the “voice of history” is frequently reduced to hatred or flattery, so the story of Sapor’s humiliations (Valerian’s shackles, the “straw‑stuffed” statue) may be more moralising than factual.  
2. **The evidence for Sapor’s cruelty is dubious** – the letters from eastern princes to Sapor are forgeries; it is unnatural for a jealous monarch to publicly degrade a rival’s majesty.  
3. **Gallienus’s character is ambiguous and self‑contradictory** – he was a brilliant but frivolous ruler, a lover of arts and philosophy rather than of war, whose public image oscillated between “effeminate” and “cruel tyrant.”  
4. **The proliferation of usurpers in the mid‑3rd century reflects the chaotic political climate** rather than a neat “thirty tyrants” parallel that the Augustan History imposes for literary effect.  

In short, the passage urges a skeptical, nuanced reading of the “tales” of Sapor and Gallienus: the moralizing narratives are partly fiction, and the political reality was one of uncertainty, personal caprice, and opportunistic usurpations.

---

## 2. Rhetorical Style

| Element | Description | Effect |
|---------|-------------|--------|
| **Allusive, learned diction** | Frequent references to classical sources (e.g., Trebellius Pollio, Hist. Aug.), medieval scholars (M. Spanheim, M. de Vallemont), and numismatic footnotes. | Demonstrates erudition; signals the writer’s place in a scholarly tradition of “critical historiography.” |
| **Balancing of admiration and criticism** | Sapor is praised for “more real monument of triumph” while also being accused of “abuse of rights of conquest.” Gallienus is praised for “lively genius” but condemned for “contemptible prince.” | Creates a nuanced portrait; the author avoids simple hero‑villain dichotomies. |
| **Use of parenthetical digressions** | Detailed footnote‑like asides on coin legends, the “straw‑stuffed” statue, the “thirty tyrants” parallel. | Engages the reader with scholarly debate; postpones judgement while providing evidence. |
| **Moral‑pathetic tone** | Describes Valerian’s “shame and grief,” the “moral and pathetic” tale, “deep sense of public disgrace.” | Evokes empathy for the Roman emperor, subtly undermining the grandeur of Persian triumph. |
| **Irony and sarcasm** | References to “effeminate prince,” “vanity of Gallienus,” “severe satire on that effeminate prince.” | Highlights the author’s critical stance toward Gallienus’s self‑image. |
| **Structured enumeration** | Long list of usurpers (nineteen names) with footnote corrections. | Gives the sense of exhaustive research; also underscores the chaotic multiplicity of claimants. |
| **Temporal shifts** | Moves from “the voice of history” → “the letters still extant” → “the reins of government held loose.” | Provides a chronological framework, showing how political looseness bred usurpations. |
| **Use of qualifiers** (“fairly,” “probably,” “not surprising”) | Softens absolute claims. | Signals cautious, provisional reasoning rather than dogmatic certainty. |

Overall, the style is **critical‑scholarly**: the author adopts the persona of a learned historian who interrogates sources, balances praise with censure, and uses extensive footnotes to demonstrate the limits of the evidence.

---

## 3. Historical Context

### 3.1. The Sapor–Valerian Episode (c. 260 CE)

* **Historical facts** – In 260 CE, the Persian king Shapur I (often called Sapor here) captured Roman Emperor Valerian during the Battle of Edessa. Valerian was taken to Persia, where he is traditionally said to have spent several years in captivity before being released on a ransom paid by his son Gallienus.  
* **Primary sources** – The *Shahriyar* (or *History of the Persians*), *Herodian* (Roman), and later *Aurelius Victor* give the story. The passage cites letters from eastern princes that the author calls forgeries, echoing modern scholarship that shows these documents are later inventions.  
* **Contemporary view** – In Roman historiography, Valerian’s captivity was a symbol of Roman humiliation; the Persians were portrayed as cruel victors. The author, however, questions that narrative, suggesting the story may be mythologised for propaganda.

### 3.2. Gallienus and the Crisis of the 3rd Century (c. 268‑275 CE)

* **Political situation** – After Valerian’s capture, the Roman Empire faced multiple usurpers, breakaway kingdoms, and external invasions (Goths, Sarmatians, Palmyrene rebels). Gallienus, son of Emperor Valerian, ruled jointly with his co‑emperor (his father) until 268, then alone.  
* **Gallienus’s reputation** – Contemporary writers (e.g., Ammianus Marcellinus) portray him as a cultured, somewhat effeminate ruler who neglected military duties. Later sources (e.g., Eutropius) emphasize his “luxury” and “indolence.”  
* **Usurpers** – The list of nineteen claimants reflects the fragmentation: Odenathus & Zenobia in the East, Posthumus, Victorinus & Victoria in the West, etc. This matches the archaeological and numismatic record of the period.  
* **Cultural milieu** – The 3rd‑century “Crisis” also saw a revival of Neoplatonism (Plotinus) and a flourishing of “philosophical” court culture, which the passage alludes to (Gallienus conversing with Plotinus, planning initiation into the mysteries of Greece).  

### 3.3. Literary Tradition

* **Augustan History** – The author references the *Historia Augusta* (a collection of imperial biographies whose authenticity is debated). The “thirty tyrants” parallel is a literary device used there to dramatise the chaos. The passage critiques this device as idle and defective.  
* **Numismatic scholarship** – The footnotes on the Gallienus coin (Gallienæ Augustæ / Ubique Pax) reveal that 17th‑century scholars (Spanheim, Vallemont) were already debating whether the coin was a satirical propaganda piece or a genuine imperial issue.  

---

## 4. Argument Structure

1. **Opening claim** – The “voice of history” often reduces itself to hatred or flattery; Sapor’s treatment of Valerian is thus suspect.  
2. **Evidence for Sapor’s cruelty** – Valerian’s shackles, the “straw‑stuffed” statue, the “more real monument of triumph.”  
3. **Counter‑evidence** – Forged letters, unnatural jealousy, the certainty that only Valerian ever fell captive.  
4. **Transition** – “At the time when the reins of government were held with so loose a hand…” introduces Gallienus.  
5. **Gallienus’s character sketch** – Brilliant in arts, weak in war, oscillating between “effeminate” and “cruel tyrant.”  
6. **Political consequences** – The “loose hand” leads to a flood of usurpers; the “thirty tyrants” parallel is an imposed literary pattern.

**Rhetorical Style**  
- **Allusion** – The passage constantly invokes well‑known Roman figures (Marius, Crassus, Pompey, Numa) and earlier literary sources (e.g., Tacitus, Suetonius) to colour contemporary events with a sense of historical gravitas.  
- **Cataloguing / Enumeration** – The author lists the “nineteen tyrants” (Tetricus, Piso, Saturninus, etc.), the qualities of “generals who assumed the title of Augustus,” and the specific vices of the armorer‑usurper Marius, creating a systematic inventory that stresses the pervasiveness of the phenomenon.  
- **Conceit (Metaphor, Simile, Hyperbole)** – “The field of victory was often the scene of their election” (metaphor for political ascent); “matchless strength” and “blunt honesty” (simile); “most savage mandate” (hyperbole) to stress the cruelty of Gallienus’s orders.  
- **Exemplum** – Concrete case‑studies (Piso’s lineage from Numa, Marius’s rise despite his low birth, the savage order against Ingenuus) serve as moral illustrations of the broader thesis.  
- **Metonymy** – “Purple” stands for imperial authority; “the armorer” for a low‑born pretender; “the field of victory” for the political arena.  
- **Hyper‑Allusion** – Multiple references to earlier texts (e.g., the classical use of “tyrannus,” the story of Marius) echo older historiographical traditions, reinforcing the author’s own argumentative stance.  
- **Enumeration (repetition of items)** – Repeated mention of “fears,” “ambition,” “disloyalty,” and “civil war” creates a rhythmic emphasis that drives home the central pattern of usurper‑driven chaos.  
- **Meta‑Commentary** – The aside “might have amused an indifferent philosopher” signals the author’s awareness of his rhetorical choices and his attempt to present a dispassionate, almost ironic analysis of events.  
- **Stereotypical Images** – The usurper is repeatedly cast as a “tyrant,” a “rebel,” or a “traitor,” drawing on contemporary moral clichés to colour the political judgment.

**Historical Context**  
The passage is a snapshot of the **Crisis of the Third Century** (c. 235‑284 CE), a period of rapid succession, civil war, and external invasion that shook the foundations of the Roman Empire. By the late 260s CE, **Emperor Gallienus** (r. 268‑275) ruled a fragmented West, while his older half‑brother **Valerian** (captured by Shapur I of Persia in 260) was effectively a prisoner. In the East, the Arab‑Palmyrene leader **Odenathus** and his daughter‑queen **Zenobia** carved out an independent realm, and a host of regional usurpers—**Tetricus**, **Piso**, **Saturninus**, **Ingenuus**, among others—rose and fell within a few months. The empire also faced relentless pressure from Germanic foederati, Sassanian Persia, and internal mutinies (e.g., the disorders of Sicily, the tumults of Alexandria, the Isaurians’ rebellion). The author draws on early modern historiographical sources such as **Tillemont** and **Brequigny** (footnote 166) to reconstruct these events, presenting them as a cascade of betrayals, donatives, and ruthless imperial edicts that drained the state’s resources.

**Main Argument**  
The author’s central claim is that the usurpers of Gallienus’s reign were **largely driven by fear rather than by genuine ambition**, and that their seizure of power was an illegal usurpation (“tyranny”) irrespective of personal virtue. He supports this by:

1. **Showing the instrumental nature of rebellion** – Most pretenders (e.g., the lieutenants of Valerian, Saturninus) rebelled because they feared Gallienus’s suspicions and the capricious violence of their troops, not because they sought power for its own sake.  
2. **Contrasting moral merit with political illegitimacy** – Figures like **Marius** and **Piso** are praised for courage and lineage, yet the author stresses that their “claim, founded on rebellion, could never obtain the sanction of law or history.”  
3. **Highlighting the destructive cost of usurpation** – The “price of their fatal elevation” was paid through massive donatives, rapine, cruelty, and the ensuing civil wars that devastated provinces and enlisted barbarian foes. The “savage mandate” of Gallienus to exterminate the male population exemplifies the regime’s ruthless policy, turning internal loyalty into external vulnerability.  
4. **Linking usurper‑driven chaos to the empire’s decline** – By cataloguing the numerous “tyrants” and their rapid rise‑and‑fall, the author illustrates how the breakdown of legitimate imperial authority accelerated the empire’s disintegration, leaving Italy, Rome, and the Senate to cling to Gallienus as the sole legitimate sovereign.  

In sum, the passage argues that the **Crisis of the Third Century** was not merely a series of external invasions but a moral and political catastrophe precipitated by a wave of illegitimate, fear‑motivated usurpations whose short‑term power grabs brought long‑term ruin to the Roman state. The rhetorical strategies employed (allusion, enumeration, metaphor, exemplary case‑studies, and meta‑commentary) serve to reinforce this judgment while simultaneously showcasing the historian’s own reflective, critical stance toward the events he narrates.

Tetricus might reign for a       while over the West, and even Zenobia might preserve the dominion       of the East. 10 These usurpers were his personal adversaries; nor       could he think of indulging any private resentment till he had       saved an empire, whose impending ruin would, unless it was timely       prevented, crush both the army and the people.

The various nations of Germany and Sarmatia, who fought under the       Gothic standard, had already collected an armament more       formidable than any which had yet issued from the Euxine. On the       banks of the Niester, one of the great rivers that discharge       themselves into that sea, they constructed a fleet of two       thousand, or even of six thousand vessels; 11 numbers which,       however incredible they may seem, would have been insufficient to       transport their pretended army of three hundred and twenty       thousand barbarians. In their passage through       the Bosphorus, the unskilful pilots were overpowered by the       violence of the current; and while the multitude of their ships       were crowded in a narrow channel, many were dashed against each       other, or against the shore. The event surpassed his own expectations and those of the world.       By the most signal victories he delivered the empire from this       host of barbarians, and was distinguished by posterity under the       glorious appellation of the Gothic Claudius. The imperfect       historians of an irregular war 13 do not enable us to describe       the order and circumstances of his exploits; but, if we could be       indulged in the allusion, we might distribute into three acts       this memorable tragedy. I. The decisive battle was fought near       Naissus, a city of Dardania. The legions at first gave way,       oppressed by numbers, and dismayed by misfortunes. Their ruin was       inevitable, had not the abilities of their emperor prepared a       seasonable relief. A large detachment, rising out of the secret       and difficult passes of the mountains, which, by his order, they       had occupied, suddenly assailed the rear of the victorious Goths.

II. We may presume that some insurmountable difficulty, the       fatigue, perhaps, or the disobedience, of the conquerors,       prevented Claudius from completing in one day the destruction of       the Goths. The war was diffused over the province of Mæsia,       Thrace, and Macedonia, and its operations drawn out into a       variety of marches, surprises, and tumultuary engagements, as       well by sea as by land. When the Romans suffered any loss, it was       commonly occasioned by their own cowardice or rashness; but the       superior talents of the emperor, his perfect knowledge of the       country, and his judicious choice of measures as well as       officers, assured on most occasions the success of his arms. The       immense booty, the fruit of so many victories, consisted for the       greater part of cattle and slaves. A select body of the Gothic       youth was received among the Imperial troops; the remainder was       sold into servitude; and so considerable was the number of female       captives that every soldier obtained to his share two or three       women. A circumstance from which we may conclude, that the       invaders entertained some designs of settlement as well as of       plunder; since even in a naval expedition, they were accompanied       by their families.

III. The loss of their fleet, which was either taken or sunk, had       intercepted the retreat of the Goths. A vast circle of Roman       posts, distributed with skill, supported with firmness, and       gradually closing towards a common centre, forced the barbarians       into the most inaccessible parts of Mount Hæmus, where they found       a safe refuge, but a very scanty subsistence. On the return of       spring, nothing appeared in arms except a hardy and desperate       band, the remnant of that mighty host which had embarked at the       mouth of the Niester.

The emperor presented Zenobia with an elegant villa at Tibur, or       Tivoli, about twenty miles from the capital; the Syrian queen       insensibly sunk into a Roman matron, her daughters married into       noble families, and her race was not yet extinct in the fifth       century. 82 Tetricus and his son were reinstated in their rank       and fortunes. They erected on the Cælian hill a magnificent       palace, and as soon as it was finished, invited Aurelian to       supper. On his entrance, he was agreeably surprised with a       picture which represented their singular history. They were       delineated offering to the emperor a civic crown and the sceptre       of Gaul, and again receiving at his hands the ornaments of the       senatorial dignity. The father was afterwards invested with the       government of Lucania, 83 and Aurelian, who soon admitted the       abdicated monarch to his friendship and conversation, familiarly       asked him, Whether it were not more desirable to administer a       province of Italy, than to reign beyond the Alps. The son long       continued a respectable member of the senate; nor was there any       one of the Roman nobility more esteemed by Aurelian, as well as       by his successors. 84

So long and so various was the pomp of Aurelian’s triumph, that       although it opened with the dawn of day, the slow majesty of the       procession ascended not the Capitol before the ninth hour; and it       was already dark when the emperor returned to the palace. The       festival was protracted by theatrical representations, the games       of the circus, the hunting of wild beasts, combats of gladiators,       and naval engagements. Liberal donatives were distributed to the       army and people, and several institutions, agreeable or       beneficial to the city, contributed to perpetuate the glory of       Aurelian. A considerable portion of his oriental spoils was       consecrated to the gods of Rome; the Capitol, and every other       temple, glittered with the offerings of his ostentatious piety;       and the temple of the Sun alone received above fifteen thousand       pounds of gold. 85 This last was a magnificent structure, erected       by the emperor on the side of the Quirinal hill, and dedicated,       soon after the triumph, to that deity whom Aurelian adored as the       parent of his life and fortunes. His mother had been an inferior       priestess in a chapel of the Sun; a peculiar devotion to the god       of Light was a sentiment which the fortunate peasant imbibed in       his infancy; and every step of his elevation, every victory of       his reign, fortified superstition by gratitude. 86

The arms of Aurelian had vanquished the foreign and domestic foes       of the republic. We are assured, that, by his salutary rigor,       crimes and factions, mischievous arts and pernicious connivance,       the luxurious growth of a feeble and oppressive government, were       eradicated throughout the Roman world. 87 But if we attentively       reflect how much swifter is the progress of corruption than its       cure, and if we remember that the years abandoned to public       disorders exceeded the months allotted to the martial reign of       Aurelian, we must confess that a few short intervals of peace       were insufficient for the arduous work of reformation. Even his       attempt to restore the integrity of the coin was opposed by a       formidable insurrection. The emperor’s vexation breaks out in one       of his private letters. “Surely,” says he, “the gods have decreed       that my life should be a perpetual warfare. A sedition within the       walls has just now given birth to a very serious civil war. The       workmen of the mint, at the instigation of Felicissimus, a slave       to whom I had intrusted an employment in the finances, have risen       in rebellion. They are at length suppressed; but seven thousand       of my soldiers have been slain in the contest, of those troops       whose ordinary station is in Dacia, and the camps along the       Danube.” 88 Other writers, who confirm the same fact, add       likewise, that it happened soon after Aurelian’s triumph; that       the decisive engagement was fought on the Cælian hill; that the       workmen of the mint had adulterated the coin; and that the       emperor restored the public credit, by delivering out good money       in exchange for the bad, which the people was commanded to bring       into the treasury. 89

We might content ourselves with relating this extraordinary       transaction, but we cannot dissemble how much in its present form       it appears to us inconsistent and incredible. The debasement of       the coin is indeed well suited to the administration of       Gallienus; nor is it unlikely that the instruments of the       corruption might dread the inflexible justice of Aurelian. But       the guilt, as well as the profit, must have been confined to a       very few; nor is it easy to conceive by what arts they could arm       a people whom they had injured, against a monarch whom they had       betrayed. We might naturally expect that such miscreants should       have shared the public detestation with the informers and the       other ministers of oppression; and that the reformation of the       coin should have been an action equally popular with the       destruction of those obsolete accounts, which by the emperor’s       order were burnt in the forum of Trajan. 90 In an age when the       principles of commerce were so imperfectly understood, the most       desirable end might perhaps be effected by harsh and injudicious       means; but a temporary grievance of such a nature can scarcely       excite and support a serious civil war. The repetition of       intolerable taxes, imposed either on the land or on the       necessaries of life, may at last provoke those who will not, or       who cannot, relinquish their country. But the case is far       otherwise in every operation which, by whatsoever expedients,       restores the just value of money. The transient evil is soon       obliterated by the permanent benefit, the loss is divided among       multitudes; and if a few wealthy individuals experience a       sensible diminution of treasure, with their riches, they at the       same time lose the degree of weight and importance which they       derived from the possession of them. However Aurelian might       choose to disguise the real cause of the insurrection, his       reformation of the coin could furnish only a faint pretence to a       party already powerful and discontented. Rome, though deprived of       freedom, was distracted by faction. The people, towards whom the       emperor, himself a plebeian, always expressed a peculiar       fondness, lived in perpetual dissension with the senate, the       equestrian order, and the Prætorian guards. 91 Nothing less than       the firm though secret conspiracy of those orders, of the       authority of the first, the wealth of the second, and the arms of       the third, could have displayed a strength capable of contending       in battle with the veteran legions of the Danube, which, under       the conduct of a martial sovereign, had achieved the conquest of       the West and of the East.

Whatever was the cause or the object of this rebellion, imputed       with so little probability to the workmen of the mint, Aurelian       used his victory with unrelenting rigor. 92 He was naturally of a       severe disposition. A peasant and a soldier, his nerves yielded       not easily to the impressions of sympathy, and he could sustain       without emotion the sight of tortures and death. Trained from his       earliest youth in the exercise of arms, he set too small a value       on the life of a citizen, chastised by military execution the       slightest offences, and transferred the stern discipline of the       camp into the civil administration of the laws. His love of       justice often became a blind and furious passion; and whenever he       deemed his own or the public safety endangered, he disregarded       the rules of evidence, and the proportion of punishments. The       unprovoked rebellion with which the Romans rewarded his services,       exasperated his haughty spirit. The noblest families of the       capital were involved in the guilt or suspicion of this dark       conspiracy. A nasty spirit of revenge urged the bloody       prosecution, and it proved fatal to one of the nephews of the       emperor. The executioners (if we may use the expression of a       contemporary poet) were fatigued, the prisons were crowded, and       the unhappy senate lamented the death or absence of its most       illustrious members. 93 Nor was the pride of Aurelian less       offensive to that assembly than his cruelty. Ignorant or       impatient of the restraints of civil institutions, he disdained       to hold his power by any other title than that of the sword, and       governed by right of conquest an empire which he had saved and       subdued. 94

| **Polysyndeton** (co‑ordinating conjunctions) | Same list as above; “and” links each activity. | Slows the rhythm, emphasizes the breadth of the celebrations. |
| **Antithesis** | “the progress of **corruption** was swifter than its **cure**” | Highlights the difficulty of reform by contrasting opposing forces. |
